cues.text: Welcome to Study Session 5 of MIT 8111, Ethics and Legal Issues in Information Technology.
This session is titled Cybersecurity Ethics and Compliance in IT, and we begin with the first chapter: cybersecurity and professional ethics.
Let us start with what cybersecurity actually is.
Cybersecurity protects information systems, networks, applications and data from threats to confidentiality, integrity and availability.
You will often see these three written together as CIA, so remember that this CIA is the security triad, not an agency.
Take each in turn.
Confidentiality restricts unauthorised disclosure, so that information is seen only by those entitled to see it.
Integrity protects accuracy and authorised changes, which means data should not be altered wrongly, and any change should be one that someone had permission to make.
Availability ensures legitimate access, meaning the people who are entitled to use a system or data can actually reach it when they need it.
Two further ideas sit alongside the triad.
Authenticity verifies identity or source, so that we can be confident who or what we are dealing with.
Non-repudiation supports evidence that an action occurred, so that a person cannot easily deny having done something.
Notice the qualification the source gives: this is subject to implementation and law.
Non-repudiation is not automatic.
How well it works depends on how a system is built, and what counts as evidence depends on the law.
Now let us get our vocabulary precise, because these words are often used loosely.
A threat is a potential cause of harm.
A vulnerability is a weakness.
Risk considers likelihood and impact, that is, how probable harm is and how serious it would be.
An incident is an event compromising or threatening security.
Pay attention to this important distinction: a vulnerability is not proof of an actual data breach.
A weakness may exist without anyone having exploited it, so we must not announce a breach merely because a flaw has been found.
Finally, controls reduce risk but cannot eliminate all uncertainty.
Safeguards help, but no professional can honestly promise perfect security.
With the technical foundation in place, we turn to ethics.
Cybersecurity ethics concerns responsible use of technical power.
People in this field can often reach systems and information that others cannot, and ethics asks how that power should be used.
The principles include public interest, non-maleficence, privacy, informed and authorised access, confidentiality, honesty, competence, fairness and accountability.
Non-maleficence means a duty to avoid causing harm.
Informed and authorised access means that access must be knowingly agreed and properly permitted.
Competence means doing the work with adequate skill, because careless security work can itself cause harm.
Accountability means being answerable for your actions.
Bringing these together, an ethical security professional protects people and systems without exceeding legitimate authority.
And here is a sentence worth remembering: technical capability or curiosity is not permission.
Being able to get into a system, or being curious about what is inside, does not give you the right to do so.
This leads naturally to security testing.
Security testing requires explicit authorisation, agreed scope, acceptable methods, time boundaries, data-handling rules, reporting and emergency stop conditions.
Let us walk through these.
Explicit authorisation means clear permission.
Agreed scope defines which systems may be tested.
Acceptable methods define what techniques are allowed.
Time boundaries define when testing may take place.
Data-handling rules govern how any information encountered is treated.
Reporting sets out how findings are communicated.
And emergency stop conditions define when testing must halt immediately, for example if it threatens to disrupt a system.
A tester must not access unrelated systems or disclose unnecessary records.
Staying within scope is an ethical duty, and it also protects the privacy of people whose data happens to be nearby.
Next, responsible vulnerability disclosure.
It involves four steps.
First, validating within authorisation, meaning you confirm the weakness only by means you are permitted to use.
Second, documenting minimally necessary evidence, so you record enough to prove the issue but no more than needed.
Third, promptly notifying responsible parties, the people able to fix the problem.
Fourth, coordinating remediation, working with them so the weakness is actually corrected.
What about timing?
Disclosure timing depends on risk, agreements, legal duties and public interest.
The source gives no fixed deadline, so we should not invent one.
One firm caution applies: do not publish exploit details or personal data indiscriminately.
Careless publication can help attackers and can expose individuals.
Finally, let us look at the familiar hat labels.
White-hat testing is authorised defensive work.
Black-hat activity is malicious or unauthorised.
Grey-hat activity may lack permission even if intent is benign.
The key lesson is that good intentions do not necessarily make access lawful.
A person who breaks in only to point out a flaw has still acted without permission, and that may be unlawful whatever the motive.
We close the chapter with dual-use knowledge.
This is knowledge that can be used both to defend and to attack.
Handling it requires context, restraint and professional judgment.
The same technique that helps a defender find a weakness could help an attacker exploit it, so a responsible professional considers who is asking, why, and under what authority.
